title: Ten cents on the prophecy: the market's likeliest woman to follow Trump promised an answer after the midterms
dek: Kalshi prices Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 10 percent to win in 2028 and 14 percent to be the Democratic nominee, behind Jon Ossoff on both boards and far ahead of every other woman. She said she would decide after the midterms. They were Tuesday. What the board says, how it got there, and what she has said.
body:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told The New York Times in September that she would decide whether to run for president after the midterms [9][11]. The midterms were Tuesday. On Friday, three days later, Kalshi's traders put her at 10 cents on the dollar to win the 2028 election and 14 cents to be the Democratic nominee, fourth and second on the two boards, and the clearest favorite among women on either [3][2]. Nobody has asked her the question yet with the excuse gone. This report is about what the market says while it waits, how it got here, and what she has said about the choice in her own words.

## The board on Friday

Kalshi's “2028 U.S. Presidential Election winner” market had Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia at 22 percent on Friday, up 3 points in a day, with Vice President JD Vance at 14 (down 1) and Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 12 (up 1) [1]. The market has traded about $87 million in contracts [1]. Below the top three, RotoWire's Thursday table of Kalshi prices ran: Ocasio-Cortez 10.0, Gov. Gavin Newsom of California 8.4, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida 6.6, Kamala Harris 3.7, James Talarico 3.0, Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky 2.9, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania 2.8, Pete Buttigieg 2.8, Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona 2.4, Gov. J.B. Pritzker of Illinois 1.9, Rahm Emanuel 1.8 and Donald Trump 1.7 [3].

On the Democratic nomination board, which has traded about $278 million, Ossoff was at 25 percent (down 1), Ocasio-Cortez at 14 (up 1) and Newsom at 12 [2]. Kalshi's party market had the Democrats at about 66 cents to win the presidency; Polymarket's global market had them at 68 [3]. Polymarket's U.S. exchange is a little warmer on Ocasio-Cortez than Kalshi: 11 to 12 cents to win, and 17 to 18 to be nominated, against 14 on Kalshi [3][4].

The exchanges' pages come with their own small print. RotoWire's table is a simple mean of last-traded prices on the two platforms, pulled through Kalshi's public API and read off Polymarket's U.S. site [3]. DeFi Rate's board, assembled Thursday evening, flags that some quotes may be stale [4]. A contract at 10 cents pays a dollar if she is inaugurated and nothing otherwise; the price is a crowd's bet, not a poll, and the crowd is small this far out.

## How she got here

In August, before the midterm campaign had properly begun, Kalshi's winner market had Vance at 19.5 cents, Rubio at 15.5, Newsom at 10.5, Ossoff at 9.8 and Ocasio-Cortez at 8.8 [5]. The Republicans held the top two spots. Then, on Aug. 9, ABC's Jonathan Karl asked her on “This Week” whether she would run, noting a New Hampshire poll that had her leading the prospective Democratic field [6]. She said she was focused on winning the midterms and did not rule it out; asked about challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer instead, she said “anything is possible at this juncture” [6][7].

The nomination market moved three points on the interview. By Aug. 13 she led it at 18 percent, with Newsom at 16 and Ossoff at 13, and Kalshi's traders put the chance that she runs at all at 66 percent [7]. Newsom's slide that week had its own cause, a Vanity Fair essay that revived a past affair [7]. Kalshi's own write-up noted that pundits had begun to take a run seriously, and that she had also left open a 2028 challenge to Schumer's Senate seat [7].

Then the board turned over. Ossoff held his Georgia seat by a wide margin on Tuesday as the party took both chambers, and the market rewarded him [13]: DeFi Rate's seven-day figures on Thursday had him up 11 points to win the presidency while Ocasio-Cortez was unchanged [4]. Vance, whose home state of Ohio sent a Democrat to the Senate and another to the governor's mansion after he campaigned heavily there, was down 4 [12][4]. She has not fallen. She has been passed.

## What she has said

The fullest account of her thinking is the Times interview, published Sept. 22. CNN's summary of it said she was weighing “everything from gender to ethnicity and her age,” and quoted her: “Pretty candidly, I think about my identity” [11]. She was 36 at the time, the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, born in the Bronx to Puerto Rican parents, and a bartender before her 2018 primary win over Rep. Joe Crowley [11]. She told the Times she had discussed the question with Harris, who was weighing a run of her own [9]. Newsom, for his part, had said he would not enter the race if Harris did [9].

The Senate is the other door. Schumer's seat is up in 2028, and she has not closed off a primary against him. Fox News, reporting on the same interview a week later, quoted her framing the decision as “Where can I do the most good?” and noted a fundraising email in which she wrote that she knew there was “a lot of speculation” about what she would decide [8]. Democratic strategists told Fox she was in a good position to win statewide, and one suggested Schumer might prefer to hand the seat to “this inspiring generational leader” rather than fight for it [8]. A presidential run is the riskier door, and she has said so: the New York Post reported her acknowledging that it is “very all or nothing,” because a loss could leave her without the House seat she holds [10].

Her allies did not wait for Tuesday. Shortly before the election, progressives formed a hybrid PAC called Ready for AOC, whose petition calls her uniquely placed to hold a coalition of the center and the left [10]. On election night, her congressional campaign sent supporters a memo arguing that her appeal runs well beyond deep-blue districts and that her small-dollar fundraising rivals Sen. Bernie Sanders's; it said allies might be asked whether she should run for president, run for Senate, or stay put, and that she “will continue to do what she's always done” [10]. Adam Green of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee told the Post that Tuesday “made the waters a lot warmer” for a run [10].

She spent the fall campaigning with mainstream Democrats as well as at Sanders's rallies, and she transferred $1 million to Abdul El-Sayed's Senate campaign in Michigan [10]. When he won, she told his supporters that if he could win in Michigan, anybody could win anywhere [10]. Not every progressive is sold; the Post noted skepticism from Cenk Uygur about her outreach to the party establishment, and some have floated Rep. Ro Khanna instead [10].

## The polls say something else

The market and the polls disagree about her, in both directions. In the RealClearPolitics average of 2028 Democratic primary polling cited by the Post, Harris leads at 24.2 percent, Newsom is at 14.2, Buttigieg at 13.1 and Ocasio-Cortez fourth at 11.8 [10]. Ossoff, the market's favorite, is not among the leaders. Harris, the polls' favorite, trades at 3 to 4 cents to win the presidency and about 5 to 8 to be nominated [3][4].

That gap is the usual one between name recognition and expected performance, and the exchanges have been on the right side of it before, but two years out it is a reminder of how much of the price is guesswork. The Simpsons prophecy that prompted these reports needs a woman to follow Trump directly. The polls' best-known woman is the one the markets have given up on; the markets' best-priced woman is the one the polls have in fourth.

## What moves the price next

Three things, in rough order of weight. First, her answer. Kalshi's August read that she runs was 66 percent, and the nomination market priced her as if she were already in [7]. An announcement would likely lift the winner contract; a Senate run against Schumer, or a decision to stay in the House, would send it toward Harris territory. Second, Ossoff. The post-midterm surge that carried him to the top of both boards is three days old and built on one night's returns [4][1]. Third, the Republican side. Vance's price fell with Ohio's results, and Trump himself, asked about 2028, said of his vice president, “Maybe he won't run,” which keeps the other side of the ledger as unsettled as this one [12].

The Watch will keep the board at [The Prophecy Watch](https://bboldt86.github.io/lanscape-navigator/news/prophecy/), with Kalshi's daily prices for the winner and nomination markets, the party line, and a running chart of the one contract that answers the Simpsons' question. On Friday the answer was 10 cents. The first report in this package explains the question; the third explains what, exactly, she would be inheriting.
